issues.subcategory: results-based abstract despite no real data
issues.description: The abstract presents inferential conclusions as if they were study findings, but the manuscript explicitly states that the results are based on a randomized dummy dataset generated only to simulate output before data collection. This makes the substantive conclusions invalid and misleading because they do not reflect observed empirical data.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: 
Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.] ... We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: methods/results based on simulated data
issues.description: The manuscript reports full methods and inferential results despite explicitly stating that these sections were written using randomized data rather than collected participant data. Any statistical test, effect size, or interpretation in the results section is therefore non-evaluable as evidence.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: 
Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: no empirical study conducted
issues.description: Because the reported sample consists of Qualtrics-generated responses rather than actual participants, the manuscript does not report a completed replication study. This is a fundamental design failure for a replication manuscript, as there are no real observations on which to assess replicability.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: fictional participant characteristics
issues.description: The participant demographics are clearly artifacts of random data generation rather than plausible sample characteristics for an MTurk replication. A mean age of 67.8 years and age range up to 120 strongly indicate simulated data, which further undermines the report's presentation as empirical results.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males). ... Age range (years) | Not specified | 18-120 | 18-120

issues.subcategory: participants self-select conditions
issues.description: The procedure states that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. This directly contradicts the claimed experimental manipulation and eliminates random assignment, introducing severe selection bias and confounding between condition and participant characteristics.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: random assignment vs self-selection contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes participants as randomly assigned to conditions, yet the procedure says they selected their preferred conditions. These are mutually incompatible descriptions of the design, preventing evaluation of internal validity.
issues.quote: In Study 1, participants were randomly assigned to two groups... In Study 3... Participants were randomly assigned to three conditions...

issues.subcategory: within-subject vs between-subject contradiction
issues.description: The design is described as a within-subject design, but all presented cell sizes sum to 1000 across six conditions, indicating a between-subject factorial design. The original studies were also between-subject. This contradiction matters because the appropriate analysis, assumptions, and interpretation differ fundamentally.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.subcategory: incorrect analysis for stated design
issues.description: If the study were truly within-subject, a standard two-way between-subjects ANOVA would be inappropriate because it ignores within-person dependence. Conversely, the cell counts indicate a between-subject design. The manuscript never resolves which structure was analyzed, so the inferential model is either wrong or inaccurately reported.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: major deviation from original donation behavior
issues.description: The original study used actual donation of earned money; this replication replaces it with an imaginary donation judgment. That changes the dependent variable from incentivized behavior to hypothetical intention, substantially weakening construct equivalence and making this not a close replication on the key outcome.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: behavioral outcome replaced with hypothetical intention
issues.description: The manuscript interprets hypothetical donation ratings as replication of actual donating behavior. Hypothetical choices may engage different motives, lower stakes, and greater social desirability than real charitable giving, so the operationalization does not cleanly match the original construct.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: different population and setting from original not integrated into claims
issues.description: The replication uses MTurk/online participants instead of people approached in a university student center, yet the manuscript still frames the study as a close-to-very-close replication and draws broad conclusions without adequately addressing the implications of this population and setting shift for replicability.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: close replication claim inconsistent with major deviations
issues.description: The manuscript classifies itself as a 'close to very close replication' despite changing the setting, population, donation incentive structure, measures, inclusion of the joint condition under intervention, and combining two original studies into one design. These are substantial departures that challenge the classification.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: explicit intervention construct altered
issues.description: The intervention is described as 'learning about prior research' and elsewhere as 'thinking analytically' or 'deliberative thinking.' Teaching participants about a named bias is not equivalent to inducing deliberation per se. This operationalization shift weakens claims about analytic reasoning as the causal mechanism.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims. ... to examine the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: conflation of bias education with analytic reasoning
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly equates explicit instruction about the identifiable victim effect with inducing a deliberative/calculative thinking mode. These are conceptually distinct manipulations; awareness of a bias does not necessarily instantiate analytic reasoning, so the theoretical interpretation is overstated.
issues.quote: The research conducted by Small et al. (2007) showed that the identifiable victim effect could be eliminated by deliberative thinking, meaning that thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation ... In Study 1 ... participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: causal language despite invalid assignment
issues.description: The manuscript makes causal claims about intervention effects, but the procedure indicates participants selected conditions themselves. Without random assignment, any differences could reflect self-selection rather than manipulation effects.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: missing actual sample recruitment and compensation details
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide essential details about actual recruitment, compensation, eligibility, or data collection because no real data were collected. Even as a protocol, the reporting is incomplete, including 'Not specified' compensation and geographic origin for the replication sample.
issues.quote:
Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified
Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: missing exclusion counts and flow
issues.description: Exclusion criteria are mentioned, but the manuscript does not report how many cases were excluded for prior knowledge or attention check failure, nor the final analyzed sample after exclusions. This prevents assessment of attrition and selection effects.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: no accounting for exclusions or missingness
issues.description: The paper mentions exclusions and presents equal condition totals summing to 1000, but never reconciles these with generated responses or reports any missing data handling. There is no participant flow, number excluded per criterion, or analytic sample derivation.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: attention check not described
issues.description: An attention check is mentioned, but its content, placement, scoring rule, and preregistered exclusion threshold are not reported. This omission precludes evaluation of whether exclusions were appropriate or could introduce bias.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: preregistration not transparently summarized
issues.description: Although the study is called preregistered, the manuscript does not clearly distinguish preregistered primary analyses from exploratory additions, nor summarize key preregistered decision rules in the paper. Multiple analyses and extensions are introduced, but the confirmatory status of each is unclear.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period. Power analyses and all materials used in these experiments are available in the supplementary materials.

issues.subcategory: multiple outcomes without multiplicity control
issues.description: The manuscript tests numerous dependent variables (donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, correlations across six conditions, multiple post-hoc tests) but provides only limited Bonferroni adjustment in some pairwise comparisons. There is no coherent familywise or false discovery control across the many inferential tests, inflating Type I error.
issues.quote: Table 9 to 18 summarise statistical testings for the hypotheses of this replication. ... We conducted a  2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions ...

issues.subcategory: effect size sign inconsistent with t statistic
issues.description: For the identifiable vs statistical comparison, the t statistic is negative, which implies the first group mean is lower than the second. Yet Cohen's d is reported as positive. The sign of d should correspond to the direction of the comparison as defined, unless explicitly using absolute values, which is not stated.

issues.subcategory: confidence interval inconsistent with significant p-value
issues.description: The post-hoc comparison is reported as statistically significant (p = .049), but the corresponding 95% confidence interval for d includes zero [-0.05, 0.20]. A two-sided 95% CI including zero is inconsistent with p < .05 for the same effect/statistic, indicating reporting or calculation error.

issues.subcategory: means reported in text do not match descriptive table
issues.description: The narrative reports means for the statistical and identifiable victim conditions that differ from the descriptive statistics table. Table 7 gives condition-specific means around 2.58/2.50 and 2.46/2.01, while the text claims identifiable M=2.24 and statistical M=2.54. These cannot be directly verified from the table and suggest averaging or transcription errors not explained in the manuscript.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: incorrect descriptive aggregation
issues.description: The means described in text for identifiable and statistical conditions do not correspond to the unweighted or weighted averages of the cell means in Table 7. This suggests either incorrect computation or failure to describe how marginal means were derived.
issues.quote:
Table 7 ... Identifiable victim condition ... 2.58 ... 2.50 ... Statistical victim condition ... 2.46 ... 2.01 ...
... participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: wrong direction of identified victim effect
issues.description: Hypothesis 1 predicts greater donation to identifiable than statistical victims, but the reported means indicate the opposite. While this could be a null or reversed finding, the manuscript does not carefully reconcile this with the stated hypothesis and original phenomenon, instead loosely describing a 'significant difference' without emphasizing it is reversed.
issues.quote: 1 (Main effect) | People donate more to an identifiable victim than statistical victims ... participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: improper contrast analysis with non-independent groups
issues.description: The manuscript compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell to the combined mean of the other five conditions using a t-test, but it does not specify whether this was implemented as a planned contrast within the ANOVA. Treating a single group versus a pooled composite as a simple t-test can be acceptable only with correct coding and variance structure; here the analysis is insufficiently specified and likely misreported.
issues.quote: we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of  identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.subcategory: missing cell-level descriptive statistics for segregated feelings
issues.description: For the significant perceived impact effect, the manuscript only provides means for two conditions in the text and no full descriptive table for all six cells. This prevents readers from evaluating pattern, variance, and interaction interpretation.
issues.quote: This suggested that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: extension hypothesis contradicted by reported results
issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable versus statistical victims, but the only significant post-hoc result is statistical versus joint, and identifiable versus statistical is nonsignificant. The abstract nevertheless claims support for the extension in a way that misstates the actual reported pattern.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims. ... Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: abstract overstates support for extension
issues.description: The abstract claims support for a hypothesis about lower perceived impact in identifiable conditions, but the formal extension hypothesis in the introduction predicts the opposite direction, and the reported post-hoc tests do not show identifiable < statistical as significant. The abstract therefore mischaracterizes both the preregistered prediction and the results.
issues.quote: 6 (Extension) | An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims ... Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: aggregated feelings composite not justified
issues.description: The manuscript aggregates heterogeneous items such as being upset, touched, sympathetic, moral responsibility, and donation appropriateness into a single 'aggregated feeling' score without theoretical or psychometric justification. Some items are emotions, others are moral judgments or evaluative beliefs, so the composite lacks clear construct validity.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling ... Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: non-affective items treated as affective feelings
issues.description: The manuscript labels moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation as affective feelings, although these are conceptually distinct appraisals or beliefs rather than emotions. This undermines the interpretation that the analyses test affective mechanisms.
issues.quote: We conducted a  2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions ... including ... moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of perceived impact as feeling variable
issues.description: Perceived impact is introduced as part of the 'feeling variables' and affective reactions, but it is more accurately a belief about efficacy. The theoretical rationale becomes muddled when cognitive efficacy judgments are conflated with emotional sympathy-based processes.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the “perceived impact of donation” as one of the feeling variables indicated in Small et al. (2007)’s Study 1.

issues.subcategory: merged studies change factorial structure
issues.description: Combining Studies 1 and 3 into one experiment and adding intervention to the joint condition creates a different design from either original study. This may alter participant interpretation and interaction structure, limiting the validity of conclusions about replication of the original findings.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention ... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.subcategory: implicit intervention not equivalent to original mechanism
issues.description: The manuscript describes the joint condition as participants 'implicitly learning about the effect,' but simply presenting both identifiable and statistical information is not equivalent to learning about the identifiable victim effect. The causal mechanism is inferred rather than directly manipulated or measured.
issues.quote: 4 (Interaction effect) | Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim ... participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: manipulation materials not reported in manuscript
issues.description: The content of the intervention, victim descriptions, and joint-condition materials are not provided in the paper, only linked externally. Without the exact wording, readers cannot assess comparability to the original manipulation or replicate the study independently.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/9sda2czfg6rzko3/AACsg1vIzXhMOInM7XMtV5ILa?dl=0

issues.subcategory: missing scale properties and response formats
issues.description: The manuscript does not report the wording, scale anchors, number of items, or reliability of the aggregated and segregated feeling measures. Without this information, psychometric adequacy and replicability cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: They were further instructed ... After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations ...

issues.subcategory: missing assumption checks
issues.description: No information is provided about whether ANOVA assumptions were checked, including normality, homogeneity of variance, or the suitability of treating bounded donation amounts and likely ordinal feeling items as continuous outcomes.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA

issues.subcategory: ordinal/bounded outcome analyzed with ANOVA without justification
issues.description: Donation is bounded from $0 to $5 and likely integer-valued; feeling items are likely Likert-type. The original paper reportedly also used ordered probit regression, but the replication omits it and uses ANOVA throughout without justification. This may distort inference when assumptions are violated.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: dropping original analytic model without rationale
issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression for donation, but the replication explicitly decides not to conduct that test and substitutes ANOVA, with no justification grounded in preregistration or measurement properties. This introduces analytic flexibility and weakens comparability to the target article.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: power analysis details omitted from manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript claims the sample size was determined by power analysis, but it does not report the target effect size, alpha, desired power, or resulting required N in the paper itself. Because the analyzed N is based on simulated data, this omission is particularly problematic.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: data collection status contradictory
issues.description: The paper states that data collection was launched and that data collection was completed before analyses, but elsewhere states the results are based on randomized simulated data and will be updated after data collection. These statements cannot all be true simultaneously.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period. ... data collection was completed before analyses. ... [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics ... These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: missing ethical approval and consent procedures
issues.description: The manuscript provides no information about ethics review, informed consent, or participant protections, despite involving human subjects and potentially charitable decision-making tasks. This is a notable reporting omission.
issues.quote: Method

issues.subcategory: overclaim from tiny and random effects
issues.description: The manuscript interprets effects from a randomized dummy dataset as if informative about theory, despite ηp² values around .006-.008 and simulated data. Even setting aside the simulation issue, such tiny effects would not warrant strong theoretical conclusions about affective heuristics or debiasing.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation ...

issues.subcategory: broad societal claims disconnected from study design
issues.description: The introduction and discussion frame the effect in terms of societal inefficiency and responses to genocide, but the replication uses hypothetical online micro-donations in a convenience sample. The manuscript does not adequately delimit inference from this narrow operationalization to broad real-world moral behavior.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation ... Solvic (2007) urged the public not to rely on our unreliable emotional responses but law enforcement to motivate actions protecting those suffering from mass murder.

issues.subcategory: table numbering/reference inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript states 'Table 7 summarizes' replication classification, but the displayed classification table is labeled Table 6. Such inconsistencies complicate interpretation and suggest insufficient manuscript quality control.
issues.quote:
Figure 2 specifies the classification of the replications ... Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication". ... Table 6

Classification of the replication

issues.subcategory: placeholder links and incomplete supplementary references
issues.description: Several project links are placeholders ('<enter link here>'), and the manuscript repeatedly refers readers to supplementary materials for essential details. This incomplete documentation limits transparency and reproducibility.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: unclear and likely incorrect confidence intervals for eta-squared
issues.description: The manuscript reports 95% CIs such as [0.00, 0.02] for ηp² from ANOVA without describing how these were computed. Given the software limitation noted and the unusual precision/truncation, the method is unclear, and the intervals may not correspond to the reported effect sizes.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: no reliability for composite feelings
issues.description: Because a composite 'aggregated feelings' score is analyzed, internal consistency (e.g., alpha/omega) should be reported. Without reliability evidence, the composite's interpretability is uncertain.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: sample table formatting/n values inconsistent
issues.description: Table 4 contains duplicated entries and formatting artifacts (e.g., '1000 | 1000', repeated sample values), making it unclear what values correspond to what columns. This undermines confidence in reporting accuracy elsewhere in the manuscript.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: misstatement of meta-analytic evidence
issues.description: The manuscript cites a meta-analytic mean effect size of 0.05 and nonetheless uses language suggesting the effect is broadly robust and crucial, without discussing that such a small average effect raises questions about practical significance and replication expectations.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05, the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial
